name: Ardkinglas Grand Fir

location.address: Ardkinglas Woodland Garden (the Pinetum), Cairndow, Argyll PA26 8BG

story:
For a number of years this was the tallest tree in Britain, the Ardkinglas estate says. The grand fir went into the lower woodland garden, the Pinetum, as a sapling around 1875. By 2002 it was recorded at 203 feet. A climber measured it at 64.28 metres in 2010, a walk report in 2014 gave 63.4, and the estate's own figure, from July 2025, is 64.8 metres. Different methods give different answers at this height, so call it around 64 metres.

The title has since moved north. The estate itself credits a Douglas fir in Reelig Glen, near Inverness, measured at 66.4 metres, with taking it, and says the record changed hands three times in a single year. Ardkinglas keeps the grand fir on its list of champion trees all the same.

The trunk was about 17 feet round in 2014, a little over five metres. We found no storm report for it, and the estate listed it as standing in 2025.

You reach it along the Window Walk, a path high above the water, a few minutes from the lochan and the bridge over the weir to the old mill. The path is hilly, with steep steps and roots. The garden is open in daylight all year, and we could not find the admission price, so check with the estate before you go. Our pin marks the garden, not the trunk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tallest conifer in the lower woodland garden, the Pinetum, about 64 metres high and five metres round. It stands along the Window Walk above the water, a few minutes from the lochan and the weir bridge.

official_register.name: Ardkinglas estate champion trees (owner page); Tree Register of the British Isles champion

access: Woodland garden open all year in daylight hours (2014 visitor account); hilly path with steep steps and roots on the Window Walk. Admission price not found on the fetched pages: check ardkinglas.com or the estate office, 01499 600261.
transport: Cairndow on the A83 at the head of Loch Fyne; no practical public transport from Glasgow beyond the Citylink Glasgow to Campbeltown coach stopping at Cairndow, check timetable. Car park at the woodland garden.
verify_notes: Pin is the centre of the OSM leisure=garden way 'Ardkinglas Woodland Garden' (Nominatim), NOT the trunk; no published GPS or OSM tree node found. Estate page: grand fir in the lower woodland garden known as the Pinetum, planted as a sapling around 1875 (estate and 2014 glasgowwestend walk both say 1875). Estate page says it was Britain's tallest tree for a number of years but has been overtaken (title said to have changed hands three times in the last year; Douglas fir at Reelig Glen Wood near Inverness 66.4 m by David Alderman and Chic Henderson, year not stated). Heights: 64.8 m as of July 2025 (estate page), 64.28 m when climbed 2010, 63.4 m (210 ft 11 in) in a 2014 walk report, 203 ft in 2002 (redwoodworld). Girth about 17 ft (glasgowwestend 2014). Reached via the Window Walk, a path high above the water, a few minutes' walk from the lochan and the bridge over the weir to the old mill. A forum comment says its top is frequently blown out; no storm-fell report found for Arwen, Eunice or Eowyn, and the estate page lists it as standing in 2025. Dates conflict slightly (planting 1875 vs height gain), heights vary by method; state as 'around 64 m'. Exact tree spot within the Pinetum unconfirmed, so approximate. Heights figures from estate page seen on fetched page.
recognise_facts: The tallest conifer in the lower woodland garden (Pinetum), reached along the Window Walk above the water, a few minutes from the lochan and weir bridge.

name: Ardkinglas Silver Fir, the Mightiest Conifer

location.address: Ardkinglas Woodland Garden, Cairndow, Argyll PA26 8BG

story:
The Ardkinglas estate calls this the mightiest conifer in Europe, and the trunk makes the case. It is a silver fir with a girth of nearly ten metres by the estate's measure, over 31 feet by Wikipedia's. The name is not new. It was given, the estate says, by the 10th Duke of Argyll more than a hundred years ago.

The estate puts it at about 250 years old. That is the owner's figure, and the only one we have, so read it as a claim rather than a count. Accounts describe the trunk dividing into several great stems, so expect a mass of timber rather than a single column.

What is missing is just as plain. No height is published. The estate does not say where in the garden it stands, so our pin marks the garden, not the tree. We found it in no storm report, and the estate still lists it among its champion trees.

Ardkinglas sits at the head of Loch Fyne, at Cairndow on the A83. The woodland garden is open in daylight all year; we could not find the admission price, so check with the estate first. The grand fir that was once Britain's tallest tree grows in the same garden, in the Pinetum.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, nearly ten metres round, which splits into several large stems. It stands in the Ardkinglas woodland garden; the estate does not publish the spot, so our pin marks the garden.

transport: Cairndow on the A83 at the head of Loch Fyne; car park at the woodland garden.
verify_notes: Estate page: 'the mightiest conifer in Europe', girth nearly 10 m, described as 250 years old, name given by the 10th Duke of Argyll more than 100 years ago. Wikipedia (Ardkinglas): girth over 31 ft (9.4 m). Trees and Shrubs Online (search snippet only, not fetched): divides into four giant ascending stems; Pakenham's Meetings with Remarkable Trees confirmed its status (unverified, snippet). Girth recorded as 940 cm (Wikipedia 9.4 m; estate 'nearly 10 m'). Age 250 is the estate's figure; it predates the 1860s-70s arboretum by the Callander family so it is probably a relic of an earlier planting; derived from a single owner claim, flagged. Spot in garden not published; pin is garden centre, approximate. Not seen in any storm report.
recognise_facts: A silver fir with a trunk nearly 10 m round that splits into several large stems, in the woodland garden; the estate names it the mightiest conifer.

name: Last Ent of Affric

location.address: Gleann nan Cichean (Glean nan Cìche), side spur of Glen Affric, near Cannich, Highland

story:
This wych elm grows out of a mountain stream, on rock with almost no soil under the moss, and it may be the last of a forest that disappeared long ago. It stands alone in Gleann nan Cichean, a side glen of Glen Affric, and Forestry and Land Scotland, who own the ground, call it hundreds of years old. Nobody has dated it more closely than that. Its trunk is 3.8 metres round at chest height.

Its loneliness has protected it. Wikipedia credits its isolation, many miles from the next elm, with keeping it free of Dutch elm disease. Somebody gave it a name from Tolkien, and in 2019 it was Scotland's Tree of the Year, nominated by Forestry and Land Scotland.

It is no longer alone. In April 2024 Forestry and Land Scotland planted 35 young wych elms from the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh beside it, inside a deer fence, the first of about 200 planned over two years. If they take, the last Ent will have a wood again.

Getting there is the real undertaking. The tree is about 11 kilometres beyond the end of the road, Forestry and Land Scotland says, with no waymarked path to it, and the road end itself is 13 kilometres of single-track from Cannich. It is a long hill walk or bike ride. Go prepared, and turn back after storms if the way looks unsafe.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone craggy elm rooted in the rocky outflow of a stream in Gleann nan Cichean. A fenced patch of young elms, planted beside it in 2024, stands next to it.

official_register.name: Woodland Trust Tree of National Special Interest; Scotland's Tree of the Year 2019 (nominated by Forestry and Land Scotland)

access: Forestry and Land Scotland ground, open access, but remote: FLS says it is hidden about 11 km from the end of the road (search result, FLS page itself not fetched with that figure). A long hill walk or bike ride beyond the Glen Affric road end; no waymarked path to the tree found. Check conditions, FLS asks visitors to turn back if unsafe after storms.
transport: Glen Affric road end car park is about 8 miles (13 km) from Cannich by single-track road; no public bus found to the road end. Cannich is reached by Inverness bus (Stagecoach/Rapsons, check timetable).

Girth 3.8 m at 1.5 m height (Wikipedia only; links Woodland Trust inventory, which this pass does not use). Age uncertain, 'hundreds of years' (FLS blog 16 Apr 2024). Probably the last survivor of an ancient forest; isolation many miles from the next elm has kept it free of Dutch elm disease. Scotland's Tree of the Year 2019, one of six finalists, public online vote, nominated by Giles Brockman of FLS. Nicknamed after Tolkien's Ents. Pin: Wikidata P625 57.22138, -5.1064 at 1e-5 precision, matches Wikipedia 57 13 17 N 5 06 23 W; treated as the trunk. No storm-fell report found. Press: Scotsman, Press and Journal on the 2019 award (not fetched). Two independent reads: FLS (landowner) plus Wikipedia citing the Woodland Trust award.
recognise_facts: A lone craggy elm rooted in the rocky outflow of a stream in Gleann nan Cichean, with a fenced patch of young elms planted beside it in 2024.

name: Benmore Redwood Avenue

location.address: Benmore Botanic Garden, A815, Benmore, near Dunoon, Argyll PA23 8QU

story:
An American planted this avenue of giant sequoias in 1863, a year after he bought the estate. James Piers Patrick lined the original drive to Benmore House with them, from seed William Lobb had brought to Britain, and more than 160 years later they are the first thing you walk through at Benmore Botanic Garden. They stand around 50 metres tall now, by the garden's own figure.

They are not well. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, which runs Benmore, says the crowns are thinning, the lower branches have lost their needles and the soil beneath them is compacted. In its words the trees are merely existing rather than growing. Since February 2021 the garden has treated the ground with geo-injection and air-lancing, and it plans a drainage raft under the grassed length of the avenue, with a public appeal to pay for the work.

How many trees make up the avenue is not settled. Figures from 49 to over 150 circulate and the garden gives none, so we will not either. Nobody has published their girth.

The avenue is just inside the entrance, so it is the start of any visit rather than a detour. Entry is paid, with children 15 and under free, and the garden is open daily from 1 March to 31 October. It is closed for the winter now and reopens on 1 March 2027. Buses run from Dunoon, which is twenty minutes by ferry from Gourock. Our pin marks the garden, not the avenue.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the double row of giant redwoods lining the original drive just inside the garden entrance. It is the first thing visitors walk through, so you cannot miss it.
access: Paid entry (RBGE): adult 12 pounds with Gift Aid, concession 10, children 15 and under free, members free. Open daily 10am to 5pm from 1 March to 31 October; closed for the season at the time of the check (4 Nov 2026), reopens 1 March 2027. The avenue is at the start of the visit, just inside the entrance.
transport: West Coast Motors bus from Dunoon to the garden (seven miles north on the A815; check timetable); Sunday shuttle from Dunoon. Dunoon is reached by CalMac or Western Ferries from Gourock in about 20 minutes.
verify_notes: Compact famous ensemble with one place to stand: the avenue of giant sequoias lining the original drive to Benmore House, right at the entrance. Planted 1863 by James Piers Patrick (an American who bought the estate in 1862), RBGE says; seed brought to Britain by William Lobb (RBGE). Height now about 50 m (RBGE; other sources say over 40 m or over 45 m). Tree count not given by RBGE (a curator says 49; another site over 150: unresolved, do not state a number). Girth not given. Condition: RBGE appeal says crowns are thinning and lower branches defoliated, soil compacted; trees are 'merely existing rather than growing'; multi-year geo-injection and air-lancing since Feb 2021, and a drainage raft planned on the grassed length of the Avenue. Alive and maintained as of the appeal page (undated). Pin is the garden coordinate from Wikipedia (56 01 35 N 4 58 52 W), not the avenue itself; avenue is at the entrance so within about 100 m: approximate. Other Benmore trees on the RBGE collection page (leads, not delivered, no locations): Douglas fir planted 1870s, 57 m, tallest at Benmore, Glen Massan Arboretum; western hemlock planted 1870s over 51 m, possibly Britain's tallest; coastal redwood planted 1872, 43.5 m; Scots pines on Golden Gates Avenue since 1820. Nominatim returns nothing for the garden name.
recognise_facts: The double row of giant redwoods lining the original drive just inside the garden entrance, the first thing visitors walk through.
